title: Redwood discovery - cost/unit economics with Tempest Capital
summary: High-level discovery focused on cost/unit economics. Tempest is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for an LLM-based research assistant. Key constraints: 5-10M tokens/month, latency SLO ~150-250ms, strict security and data residency for client data, and a conservative budget. Discussed per-token pricing, batching and prefix/KV caching levers, quantization tradeoffs, and pilot plan. Agreed next steps: send pricing + batching guidance, share SOC2/security docs, schedule SE-led deep-dive and prototype benchmark.
action_items: Lena Morales: Send detailed pricing sheet and cost model + example unit economics - due 2026-10-12
Raj Patel: Draft pilot benchmark plan (throughput/latency targets, sample prompts) and propose compute config - due 2026-10-14
Maya Zhang: Share sample workload, average prompt lengths, and retention requirements - due 2026-10-09
next_steps: Schedule dedicated technical deep dive with infra team (Raj + Derek)
Run pilot with 5M token/mo estimate and compare Hosted vs Dedicated cost
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-07
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Lena Morales (Redwood AE), Raj Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Zhang (Tempest Head of MLOps), Ethan Cole (CTO), Derek Lin (Infra)
Links referenced: pricing deck (link), security packet / SOC2 (link), sample benchmark sheet (link)

Auto-summary (auto): Discussed economics of hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments; focused on per-token unit costs, batching/caching levers, and a pilot to validate latency/cost tradeoffs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Lena from Redwood, with me is Raj our systems SE. How are you all?
[00:08] Maya: Good thanks, Maya here. We run ML infra for Tempest's research assistant product. Ethan and Derek are on as well.
[00:15] Ethan: Hey all. High level — we want to understand cost per token and if we can hit latency targets for interactive queries.
[00:22] Raj: Great. Quick agenda: pricing overview, batching and caching levers, hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, then identify next steps and pilot plan.
[00:29] Derek: Sounds good. For context our rough usage is 5M tokens/month initially, scaling to maybe 10M. Average prompt + response is 300 tokens, peak concurrency ~30 reqs/s. Latency target for UI is 150-250ms 95th. Security is strict, some docs need to remain in EU region.
[00:45] Lena: Thanks — that's perfect. On pricing we have per-token pricing on Hosted, and with Dedicated you get reserved capacity with a commit which changes unit economics. We'll send the detailed sheet but high-level — hosted is simplest but unit price is higher; Dedicated is lower per-token once you hit commit levels, and Private adds more infra/ops cost but satisfies regulatory constraints.
[01:04] Maya: Can you quantify "higher"? Like 2x, 3x? Our budget is pretty tight.
[01:09] Lena: Sure — ballpark for a 13B-class open model: hosted might be around $0.0009 per prompt-token and $0.0009 per completion-token combined, whereas Dedicated can push equivalent unit cost down by 30-60% depending on utilization, batching, and whether you use quantized instances. I'll follow up with specific numbers for the model you pick.
[01:28] Ethan: That range is helpful. Where does batching come in? We assume more batching reduces cost but increases latency.
[01:33] Raj: Exactly. Continuous batching and adaptive batching are two levers. For small interactive workloads, you can enable micro-batching — Redwood's runtime supports sub-100ms batching windows to group tokens. There's also automatic prefix/KV caching which can avoid recomputing shared prefixes across requests — that is big for conversation-style or templated prompts.
[01:52] Derek: Is that K-V cache persistent across requests or per-connection?
[01:55] Raj: It's prefix/KV caching — persistent at the serving layer for reuse across requests when prompts share prefixes. We also have session caches for chat contexts. Note sometimes transcript reads it as K-V cash in our exported notes ha.
[02:06] Maya: Ha, noted. How much does caching typically drop token cost?
[02:10] Raj: It depends. For heavy prefix reuse, we've seen effective token savings of 20-60% in production. For templated queries it can be dramatic. Batching can reduce GPU idle time and improve throughput; that often yields 10-40% cost improvements depending on model and sequence length distributions.
[02:29] Ethan: What about quantization? We tend to use trimmed float16 models in-house. If we quantize to 4-bit, how does that change economics and latency?
[02:36] Raj: Quantization reduces memory footprint so you can run larger models per GPU and improves throughput — usually better unit cost. There's sometimes a small latency improvement due to better packing, but quantization can slightly degrade output quality especially for sensitive research tasks. For many use cases, 4-bit or mixed quant is a good tradeoff. We'll include recommendations per model.
[02:54] Maya: Region/residency: we need EU-only for some clients. Hosted supports region pinning?
[02:59] Lena: Our Hosted API has region options in EU and NA; for strict residency and control, Dedicated or Private is better because you can reserve capacity in an EU region or deploy Private in your VPC. That adds platform and infra costs.
[03:12] Derek: For Dedicated, what's the onboarding and lead time? If we commit to a reserved pool, how fast can we get it live?
[03:18] Lena: Typical lead time is 2-6 weeks depending on capacity and config. We also offer burst capacity to handle spikes.
[03:25] Ethan: For our 5M tokens/month estimate, do you have a simple cost model we can run?
[03:30] Raj: Yes — we usually model cost as: billable tokens times per-token price adjusted by effective utilization and cache hit rate, plus a reserved capacity monthly fee for Dedicated. I'll send a spreadsheet that lets you plug in prompt length, cache hit %, batching efficiency, and compute mix.
[03:47] Maya: On batching efficiency — is there a way to get real numbers from us without a full pilot? Some heuristics would help.
[03:53] Raj: We have historical heuristics: for average prompt+response ~300 tokens, with peak concurrency 30, you'd likely see batching efficiency around 1.2-1.6x on throughput for hosted continuous batching; Dedicated with optimized compiles can get 1.5-2.5x depending on kernel choices. But we should run a short benchmark.
[04:12] Ethan: What's the expected latency delta between Hosted and Dedicated for the same model?
[04:16] Raj: Dedicated often has lower median and 95th latencies because of reserved GPU scheduling and optimized kernels — maybe 10-30% lower 95th depending on contention. But it's workload dependent. We'll test with your sample prompts.
[04:29] Derek: On the infrastructure side — for Private, do you manage the control plane? Or is it fully customer-managed?
[04:34] Lena: For Private we offer a customer-managed data plane and an optional private control plane. You can also choose an on-prem package if you need air-gapped. We'll include architecture notes in the security pack.
[04:46] Maya: Security questions — we need SOC2, SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs, KMS/HSM integration. Are those available out of the box?
[04:54] Lena: Yes — SOC2 is available; SSO/SAML and RBAC are standard on Dedicated/Private; audit logs and KMS integrations are available; we'll share the security packet.
[05:02] Ethan: Back to cost — do you have examples of customers who moved from Hosted to Dedicated and the inflection point?
[05:09] Lena: Typically teams commit to Dedicated when monthly usage goes above a few million tokens and they need predictable latency or data isolation. The spreadsheet I'll send shows a break-even point given assumed utilization and caching.
[05:21] Maya: OK let's talk pilot. We want to run a 2-week pilot to compare Hosted vs Dedicated cost and latency with our sample workload. Can Redwood stand up both?
[05:29] Raj: We can do a Hosted benchmark immediately; for Dedicated we can spin a small reserved instance or use a pre-configured test pool for the pilot. We'll need sample prompts, an S3 bucket or sample dataset, and an access plan.
[05:41] Derek: On instrumentation — we need token-level cost and latency breakdowns. Do you expose per-route dashboards?
[05:46] Raj: Yep — Redwood Console gives token-level cost, per-model breakdowns, trace links, and error rates. You'll get a dashboard for the pilot.
[05:54] Ethan: Any gotchas we should be aware of around caching and prompt design that affect measurements?
[05:58] Raj: Yes — if prompts include per-user unique prefixes, caching benefits are lower. Also long context windows change kernel selection; you'll see different throughput/latency. We'll advise on prompt templating and batching-friendly patterns.
[06:12] Maya: For the pilot, what metrics should we measure? Latency p50/p95, tokens per second, cost per 1k tokens, cache hit rate?
[06:18] Raj: Exactly. Also measure tail latency, percent of requests batched, GPU utilization, and model output quality metrics if you have eval prompts.
[06:27] Lena: Quick commercial note — we can provide a short-term pilot discount or credits to offset the benchmark cost, depending on the commitment. I'll include options in the pricing email.
[06:36] Ethan: Great. On timeline — if we can get pricing and pilot plan this week, we can start the pilot next week.
[06:42] Lena: We'll aim to send pricing and the pilot plan by Monday. Raj will draft the technical plan.
[06:48] Maya: One more question — how is preemptible or spot capacity handled for Dedicated?
[06:52] Raj: We support burst into lower-cost preemptible capacity for non-latency-critical workloads; for strict SLOs you can pin to on-demand reserved pools. We'll map options in the cost model.
[07:04] Derek: Any notes on multi-model routing or fallbacks if a model is unavailable?
[07:08] Raj: Smart routing supports fallbacks to compatible model variants (e.g., from 13B quant to 7B or different quant levels) to keep the app online. That can be part of an autoscaling/fallback policy.
[07:18] Ethan: OK sounds good. Are you able to share an example cost calc for our 5M tokens?
[07:22] Lena: We'll share an example. Ballpark — with caching and batching assumptions you could see X cost on Hosted and maybe 35-50% lower on Dedicated at the same utilization. But exacts will be in the sheet.
[07:33] Maya: Cool. If we do Dedicated what about hardware selection — A100 vs H100 vs ML accelerators — any preference?
[07:39] Raj: H100s give better throughput for larger models and better kernel support for certain attention patterns; A100 is still cost-effective. We'll recommend hardware based on sequence length distribution and model (we'll run microbenchmarks).
[07:52] Ethan: Quick flag — procurement will want T&Cs; can you share standard terms and a rough MSA?
[07:58] Lena: Yes we'll include procurement path and standard MSA template.
[08:03] Derek: Ok last thing: retention and logs — can we control retention windows for logs and metrics?
[08:08] Raj: Yes — Console lets you configure retention and export logs to your SIEM or S3.
[08:14] Lena: Seems like we have clear next steps. Raj, you'll own the pilot plan. I'll send pricing and the security packet. Maya, you'll provide sample prompts and token estimates.
[08:23] Maya: Yep I'll share the sample set and expected traffic shape.
[08:26] Ethan: Thanks, that's helpful.
[08:28] Lena: Great thanks everyone. Quick recap: Lena to send pricing + security docs; Raj to draft pilot plan; Maya to share workload; follow-up for deep technical meeting.
[08:40] (call ends)

Notes about transcript quality: Automatic captions mis-heard "KV cache" once as "K V cash", Redwood product "Dedicated" sometimes written as "Dedicate"; proper nouns like some internal model names were fuzzy.

End of file.
